extracted.intended_audience: drama teachers, theatre educators, improvisation practitioners, and students interested in TheatreSports/competitive improvisation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical context for running, teaching, and evaluating TheatreSports and competitive improvisational drama in educational and community settings, including scoring, pedagogy, content rules, and desired learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience scoring (0–5) by judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges (often audience members) hold up cards scored from 0 to 5 based on their personal and emotional gut responses to the humour and inherent risks of the scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numbers are tallied on a scoreboard for everyone to see; early TheatreSports used hand-drawn numbered cards. Some formats pick audience members as judges; televised formats sometimes award quick or seemingly random points (criticised in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting offers / move the scene forward
rubrics_metrics.description: One fundamental is to move the scene forward by accepting the offers and ideas of the other people on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progression depends on building on others' contributions; accepting offers is a basic technical strategy that students can master and implement in future theatrical projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking (definition and impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stopping a scene from progressing is called 'blocking' and takes all the energy out of improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocking is an attribute quickly done away with in teaching and competition; it's identified as harmful to scene momentum and is treated as an evaluative negative (implicitly penalized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content restrictions: no sexism, racism, swearing, homophobic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation work in many educational/competitive contexts explicitly excludes sexism, racism, swearing, and homophobic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students and teams are penalized (by deducting points or by losing stage time) if they indulge in any of these areas; this is noted as a deliberate departure from other drama teaching approaches that rely on self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain pedagogical rigor and methodological framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv should not be reduced to watered-down, pabulum-like games without rationale or methodological framework; teaching must avoid lazy delivery that undermines drama as substantive curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against spending an entire year doing TheatreSports merely for ease of delivery; teachers should provide rationale, methods, and structure to avoid developing 'sloppy student improvisers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation beyond laughs and clever endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Success should not be evaluated solely on the volume of laughs or clever, clichéd, pithy endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of superficial assessment practices: encourage evaluation of structure, storytelling, risk-taking, and authenticity rather than only audience amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good improvisers are good storytellers
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnstone and the author argue that good improvisers must be good storytellers; newer narrative forms (e.g., Micetro Impro, Guerilla Theatre) rely heavily on storytelling techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should cultivate storytelling skills (narrative structure, detailed forms) in improvisation training to deepen artistic content beyond short challenge games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interactivity: energize vs. enable self-indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive audience participation (suggestions, cheering, jeering, throwing props) can create invigorating theatrical experiences but also risks promoting insincere or self-indulgent improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a referee, master of ceremonies, or coaxing actors can harness audience energy; instructors should be aware of the double-edged nature and manage interactivity to avoid 'gutless light entertainment'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition as motivational tool with educational drawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning process-oriented improvisation into competition can motivate students and provide public recognition, but it raises questions about benefits and drawbacks to the original exploratory purpose of improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition can compel participation (especially in competitive school cultures) and help marginalised curricula gain recognition, yet teachers should balance competitive formats with curricular learning objectives and not let competition trivialize pedagogical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and transparency of adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication methods vary—from audience-judge card systems to seemingly random televised points—and affect perceived fairness and educational value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian Improv Games and some competitions choose audience judges and explicit scoring; the text criticises formats where scoring appears capricious (e.g., TV shows), suggesting structured, transparent judging is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical strategies and transferable skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv games provide basic technical strategies (e.g., acceptance, moving scenes forward) that can be mastered and applied to future theatrical projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure of many games makes sense pedagogically; teachers should emphasize these teachable techniques rather than treating games as mere pastime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational and developmental outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation supports spontaneity, risk-taking, creative and critical thought, empathy, role-taking, insight, and the ability to 'live in the moment'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as curricular objectives since the 1960s, improvisation is framed as facilitating social and psychological growth, increased awareness, and opportunities for students who may avoid scripted performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating a fun, trusting, cohesive learning community
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective drama/improv teaching fosters a fun, trusting, and cohesive community of learners to connect students both as active participants and audience members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social environment supports inclusion and enables students of varying comfort with scripted work to engage productively in theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding commercialization/degradation of original intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that dissemination and popularisation (e.g., television formats, cheap imitations) can misinterpret or forget the original pedagogical/artistic intentions behind TheatreSports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers and practitioners should seek to preserve Keith Johnstone's deeper methodologies and rationale rather than adopt only the entertaining surface features.
